Question: description: Imposing trade defence measures (anti-dumping, countervailing duties and safeguards) on ICT-related products imported by other Asia-Pacific economies
Source Legislation:
Regulation of the Minister of Trade No.34/M-DAG/PER/6/2014 on Antidumping Measure, Compulsory Measure, and Trade Safeguard Measure 2011;

Komite Anti Dumping Indonesia (KADI) website
Impact:
Regulation of the Minister of Trade of the Republic of Indonesia Number 34/M-DAG/PER/6/2014, primarily outlines the organization and work procedures of the Indonesian Trade Security Committee (KPPI). It does not explicitly mention ICT-related goods (Information and Communication Technology) or any specific articles related to ICT. Instead, it provides a general framework for handling trade security measures, including investigations into serious losses or threats to domestic industries caused by surges in imports.

- Article 2: KPPI is tasked with addressing issues related to serious losses or threats to domestic industries caused by a surge in imports. If ICT-related goods are identified as causing such issues, KPPI would handle the investigation.
- Article 3: KPPI's functions include: Conducting investigations into serious losses or threats to domestic industries caused by imports. Collecting and processing evidence related to such investigations. Recommending trade security actions to the Minister of Trade.
- Article 12: The Sub Committee of Investigation in the Sector of Industry and Mining is responsible for investigating serious losses or threats to domestic industries in the industrial and mining sectors. ICT-related goods, being part of the industrial sector, could fall under this category.
- Article 14: Financing for KPPI's activities, including investigations into specific goods (potentially ICT-related), is covered by the National Budget of the Ministry of Trade.

From the Penyelidikan Berjalan (Ongoing Investigations) section of the KADI website, there are currently no explicit cases related to ICT (Information and Communication Technology) goods. The ongoing investigations listed are:
- PP Copolymer
- Benang Filamen Sintetik (Synthetic Filament Yarn)
- Kertas Duplex (Duplex Paper)
- PP Homopolymer

Question: description: Foreign exclusions from public procurement related to ICT goods and digital services
Source Legislation: Presidential Regulation No.16 on Government Procurement of Goods and Services 2018
Impact:
The Presidential Regulation No.54 on Government Procurement of Goods and Services 2010 has been revoked and replaced by Presidential Regulation 16/2018 where there is currently a second revision of Presidential Regulation 16/2016 (amendment) 

Presidential Regulation No.16 Year 2018 on Government Procurement and its amendments:
-	The Presidential Regulation underlines the importance of key procurement principles, such as transparent, open, effective, competitive and accountable as well  as value for money.
-	According to article 63, foreign companies may participate in international procurement under the following thresholds:
○	Rp 1 trillion (approx. 60.8 million USD*) for construction works;
○	Rp50 billion (approx. 3.01 million USD*) for goods and other services; and
○	Rp25 billion (approx. 1.52 million USD*) for consulting services.
-	Furthermore, foreign companies are also allowed to participate under such thresholds in a case there are no qualified domestic companies to fulfill requirements/technical specification. Therefore, the participation of foreign companies is not restricted to extremely large bids.
-	In the same article, it is stipulated that international procurement is announced on the website of the Ministries/Institutions/Local Governments and the international community website. 

Article 66 mentions the use of domestic products in government procurement, however, there is also the possibility to procure imported goods in the event that the goods cannot be produced domestically or domestic production volume is unable to meet the demand.

Foreign business actors can also participate in procurement in Indonesia below a predetermined threshold value as long as there are no capable and qualified national business actors. This means that Indonesian government procurement does not exclude foreign business actors in general or a group of foreign business actors or only allow foreign business actors for procurement packages above the threshold.

Question: description: Foreign exclusions from public procurement related to ICT goods and digital services
Impact:
Under the Regulation of the Government of the Republic of Indonesia No.29 of 2018 on Industrial Empowerment 2018 as amended by Government Regulation (PP) No.28 of 2021
Maintenance of Industrial Fields, Articles 57 and 58 specify the obligation of utilizing domestic products for government procurement if funded by the state or regional budgets, including details on compliance.

According to Article 57, the following entities are required to utilize domestic products in the procurement of goods and services: State institutions, ministries, non-ministerial government institutions, other government institutions, and regional working units when the procurement is financed by:
- The state budget (APBN) or regional budget (APBD).
- Domestic or foreign loans or grants.
State-owned enterprises (SOEs), other state-owned legal entities, regionally-owned enterprises, and private enterprises in the procurement of goods and services when:
- Financing is derived from the state budget or regional budget.
- Work is conducted under a cooperation scheme between the Central Government and/or Local Governments with enterprises.
- The procurement involves the exploitation of state-controlled resources (e.g., natural resources, telecommunications frequencies, etc.).

Article 58 specifies that the obligation to utilize domestic products applies at both the planning and implementation stages of the procurement process.
Entities must prepare an annual plan for the goods and services they need, including technical specifications, amounts, prices, and procurement schedules. 

Article 61 requires that domestic products must be utilized if the combined value of their National Contribution Value (TKDN) and Corporate Contribution Value is at least 40%. The TKDN value of the domestic product must be at least 25%.

Article 64 mandates price preferences for domestic products:
- A maximum 25% price preference for goods with a TKDN value of at least 25%.
- A maximum 7.5% price preference for construction services provided by domestic companies over foreign competitors.

Question: description: Foreign exclusions from public procurement related to ICT goods and digital services
Source Legislation: Regulation of the Minister of Communication and Informatics of the Republic of Indonesia No.41/PER/M.KOMINFO/10/2009 on Procedures for Assessing the Achievement of Domestic Component Levels in the Implementation of Telecommunications 2009
Impact:
Decree No. 41/PER/M.KOMINFO/10/2009: Article 1(4) and subsequent sections define and outline the procedures for assessing domestic content (TKDN) in telecommunications.
Article 1(4): Definition of Level of Domestic Component (TKDN). TKDN (LDC) is defined as the portion of domestic components in goods, services, or a combination of both, used in telecommunications.
It includes:
- Goods: Telecommunication materials and equipment.
- Services: Design, engineering, and other supporting services.
- Combination: A mix of goods and services.
The domestic component must involve local manufacturing, fabrication, assembling, work settlement, and services performed domestically, using local experts and software.

Article 3(1) and 3(2) of Calculation of TKDN and Foreign Component provides the formula for calculating the Level of Domestic Component (TKDN) and explicitly identifies the Foreign Component (FC) as part of the calculation. The formulas are:

Formula 1:
% TKDN (Capex) = ((Total Capex − Foreign Component Capex) /Total Capex) × 100 %

Formula 2:
% TKDN (Capex) = (Domestic Component Capex / Total Capex) ×100%

This explicitly separates foreign components (e.g., imported goods, foreign services, foreign software) from domestic components, ensuring that foreign elements are excluded from the TKDN percentage.

Article 4(1) and 4(2) of Proof of Domestic Expenditure requires telecommunication providers to show proof of domestic expenditure for telecommunication materials/equipment sourced from domestic vendors. It also mandates that the percentage of TKDN for these materials/equipment must be authenticated by:
- An authorized agency or
- An independent survey institute assigned by the government.
This ensures that foreign components are excluded unless they are explicitly verified as domestic.

Article 5 of Verification of Domestic Components  mandates that any assessment of TKDN using telecommunication materials/equipment from domestic providers must be verified by:
- An authorized agency, or
- An independent survey institute.
This verification process ensures that foreign components are not misrepresented as domestic.

Article 6 of Local Content Threshold states that telecommunication materials/equipment with ≥ 50% local content are considered to have 100% local content for TKDN purposes. This provision effectively excludes foreign components from being counted as domestic unless they meet the 50% threshold.

Question: description: Foreign exclusions from public procurement related to ICT goods and digital services
Source Legislation: Regulation of the Minister of Industry No. 15/M-IND/PER/3/2016 on Specification Standards and Price Standards for Domestic Transmission Towers and Conductors to Accelerate the Development of Electricity Infrastructure 2016
Impact:
Regulation No. 15/M-IND/PER/3/2016 primarily focuses on Tower Transmission and Conductor products, the principles outlined in Articles 2, 4, 6, 7, and 8 regarding the prioritization of domestic content (TKDN) and compliance monitoring can be applied to ICT goods and digital services in public procurement.

Article 2 states that Tower Transmission and Conductor products must comply with Standar Spesifikasi (Standard Specifications) and Standar Harga (Standard Prices). The specifications and pricing standards are likely designed to favor domestic products, indirectly excluding foreign goods that do not align with these standards.

Article 4 establishes a benchmark pricing system for the procurement of domestic Transmission Towers and Conductors. This ensures that public procurement adheres to fair and consistent pricing, avoiding overpricing or underpricing. By mandating adherence to Standard Prices for domestic products, Article 4 indirectly excludes foreign products that may not align with these price benchmarks. This is because foreign products are not explicitly included in the pricing standards, and the regulation prioritizes domestic goods. The Standard Prices are tied to the domestic content requirements (TKDN) outlined in Article 6. 

Article 6 article mandates that Tower Transmission and Conductor products used in the acceleration of electricity infrastructure must meet a minimum Tingkat Komponen Dalam Negeri (TKDN) (Domestic Component Level) of 40%. This provision explicitly prioritizes domestic products and components, effectively excluding foreign goods and services that do not meet the required TKDN threshold from public procurement, because only products meeting the minimum TKDN threshold (40%) are eligible for procurement, and their prices must align with the standards in Lampiran I and II.

Article 7: The TKDN value must be verified and certified through a formal process, as outlined in this article. Ensuring that only products meeting the domestic content requirements are eligible for procurement, further excluding foreign products that fail to meet these standards.

Question: description: Specific requirements on source codes, encryption and trade secrets
Source Legislation: Regulation of the Government of the Republic of Indonesia No.71 on the Provision of Electronic System and Transaction 2019
Impact:
Government Regulation No. 82 of 2012 on the Implementation of System and Electronic Transactions. Specifically, Article 8: Requires that providers who develop software specifically for a government agency must submit the source code and related documentation to the agency. If direct submission is not feasible, the source code and documentation should be entrusted to a reliable third party. We are of the view that the notes contained in the column Findings/ Inquiries regarding the sub-pillars may provide some insight into the content of Article 8. Article 9: Emphasizes the confidentiality of the source code, allowing for inspection only if necessary for investigation purposes. 

Government Regulation No. 71 of 2019 on the Implementation of System and Electronic Transactions regarding the Implementation of Electronic Systems and Transactions, article 9 specifies that software developers providing custom software for public electronic systems must submit source code and documentation to the relevant public institution. If internal storage is not feasible, a third party trusted for source code safekeeping can be used. This ensures government institutions maintain control over critical software. This regulation do not explicitly link trade secrets to public procurement but imply the need for protecting sensitive information. For instance, Article 15 emphasizes maintaining the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of personal data and related documentation. The first and second sentences in bullet point 2.2.1(a) are true because can be referred to Article 9 paragraph (1) and (3). However, the next sentence is an author's interpretation that is not included in the body or explanatory section of PP 71/2019.

Based on Article 103 paragraph (2) of Government Regulation No. 71/2019, Government Regulation No. 82/2012 has been revoked. Therefore, following the legal principle lex posterior derogat legi priori (a newer regulation overrides an older one), the provisions under Government Regulation No. 71 of 2019 now serve as the main legal reference for the implementation of electronic systems and transactions.

Question: description: Limitations in procurement bidding
Source Legislation: Regulation of the Minister of Industry No.02/M-IND/PER/1/2014 on Guidelines of Increasing Use of Domestic Products 2014
Impact:
The Ministry of Industry Regulation No. 02/M-IND/PER/1/2014 Article 16.1 restricts the participation of foreign suppliers in public procurement. According to the law, Articles 17 and 20 discuss the Domestic Component Level (TKDN) and the Benefit to Company Points (BMP) which is based on investments of the suppliers in Indonesia. According to Article 10, domestic service suppliers need to be prioritized. To be considered as a domestic service supplier, the majority of shares have to belong to an Indonesian citizen and two-thirds of the board members have to be locals. If no domestic service suppliers are participating in the procurement, service suppliers where more than 50% up to 90% is owned by a foreign company or foreign citizen will be taken into consideration. 

Ministry of Industry Regulation No. 02/M-IND/PER/1/2014: Article 3 and Article 4 cover the guidelines for the promotion and mandatory use of domestic products in government procurement, detailing conditions for verifying TKDN values. Article 10 mandates that service procurement must prioritize home services companies, which must be established under Indonesian law and operate domestically, with more than 50% shareholding by Indonesian citizens or state entities, and two-thirds of the board comprising Indonesian citizens. Articles 15 and 16 allow for participation by foreign service companies when domestic or national service companies are unavailable, specifying that such foreign companies can participate under specific conditions.

Question: description: Limitations in procurement bidding
Source Legislation: Regulation of the Government of the Republic of Indonesia No.71 on the Provision of Electronic System and Transaction 2019
Impact:
Government Regulation No. 71/2019 states that the electronic systems operators for public scope should store the electronic transaction data in Indonesia, unless the technology needed is unavailable in Indonesia. Public ESOs are defined to include 
(a) public bodies (such as central and regional executive, legislative, judicative bodies and any other bodies established pursuant to a statutory mandate); and 
(b) entities appointed by public bodies to operate electronic systems on their behalf. Previously, Government Regulation 82 (Article 17) required “electronic systems operators for public service” to connect their data to a data centre and a disaster recovery centre established in Indonesian territory for law enforcement and data protection. 

Although “public services” was not defined under the Government Regulation 82, this term had been interpreted in practice by MOCI broadly. Therefore, the local storage obligations were widely understood to cover all services offered to the public via the internet, effectively affecting many private sector companies.

Note that Government Regulation No. 82 of 2012, replaced by Government Regulation No. 71/2019 regarding the Provision of Electronic System and Transaction.

Domestic products and services are defined as goods or services produced or prepared by a company investing and producing in Indonesia, with the possibility to use imported raw material or component in the production or working process.

Question: description:
Foreign equity limits in sectors relevant to digital trade 
Exception: Not cover foreign equity cap in telecom sector (covered under Pillar 5) and e-commerce sector (covered under Pillar 12)
Source Legislation: Law No. 25 on Investment 2007
Impact:
Indonesia's Investment Law No. 25 of 2007 provides a broad legal framework for investment in Indonesia, emphasizing openness and equal treatment to foreign investment (Article 6) while allowing for specific restrictions in certain sectors. For precise foreign equity limits in sectors relevant to digital trade, one would need to refer to the Positive Investment List and the Presidential Regulation No. 10 of 2021. The “Positive Investment List,” is part of Indonesia’s broader strategy to attract foreign investment while protecting specific sectors for local businesses. The Positive Investment List allows 100% foreign ownership in several key areas to encourage foreign investment in digital infrastructure and technology (listed in the annexes). 

This includes large-scale e-commerce platforms, classified under high-capital investment thresholds, which enable global players to operate independently, and data centers (Business Field No. 63111), which are critical for supporting Indonesia’s digital economy and data storage needs. Additionally, cloud computing services for general use are open to full foreign ownership, allowing flexibility for international technology companies to provide cloud services in Indonesia. Over-the-top (OTT) digital content platforms, such as video and music streaming services, are also unrestricted, promoting the growth of diverse content services for Indonesian consumers. These policies align with Indonesia’s digital transformation goals by enhancing technology transfer, infrastructure development, and consumer access to global digital services, while maintaining regulatory oversight for sectors with more strategic or sensitive data requirements, such as critical infrastructure and payment systems.

Source Legislation: Law No.32 on Broadcasting 2002
Impact:
Law No. 32 of 2002 on Broadcasting prohibits foreign equity ownership in terrestrial (free-to-air) broadcasting companies “Broadcasting agencies may be established by Indonesian legal entities, and foreign parties are prohibited from participating in the ownership of broadcasting agencies.” Broadcasting agencies are to operate in accordance with national interests, implying that foreign ownership is restricted to ensure cultural sovereignty. Covers terrestrial television and radio broadcasting companies but does not apply to subscription-based services like cable or satellite broadcasting.

- Article 16 states (1) the Private Broadcasting Institution as referred to in Article 13 paragraph (2) letter shall be a commercial broadcasting institution in the form of a juristic person established under Indonesian law, whose field of business shall only operate radio or television broadcasting services. (2) Foreign nationals shall be prohibited from being in the management of Private Broadcasting Institution, except for finance and technical fields.
- Article 17 states (1) the Private Broadcasting Institution as referred to in Article 16 paragraph (1) shall be established, the initial capital of which is wholly owned by Indonesian citizens and/or juristic persons established under Indonesian law. (2) Private Broadcasting Institution may make additions and developments in fulfilling the capital derived from foreign capital, which amounts to no more than 20% (twenty percent) of the total capital and is owned by a minimum of 2 (two) shareholders.
- Article 23 states (1) Community Broadcasting Institution shall not receive initial establishment funds and operational funds from foreign parties.
- Article 30 states (1) Foreign broadcasting institutions shall not be established in Indonesia.

Impact:
There is a limit of 49% on the shares that can be acquired by foreign investors in government-controlled firms. This includes foreign participation to SOEs in telecommunication and delivery service sectors (as regulated in the Government Regulation No. 15/2013 amended by the Government Regulation No.41/2021).

The Government Regulation No. 15 of 2013, as amended by Government Regulation No. 41 of 2021, regulates the foreign ownership limit for State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs) and their subsidiaries. This regulation emphasizes maintaining government majority control in strategic sectors. The 49% cap is designed to attract foreign investment and expertise while keeping majority ownership within the Indonesian government.

The Telecommunications and Delivery Service  sectors are classified as “strategic sectors” that are subject to heightened restrictions due to their importance to national security and public access. In these sectors, SOEs may have foreign partners, but the government generally maintains a 51% ownership or controlling interest in these enterprises.

Source Legislation: Regulation of Financial Services Authority No.12/POJK.03/2021 of 2021 on Commercial Banks 2021
Impact:
Foreign ownership in banks is governed under Financial Services Authority Regulation (POJK) 12/2021 on Commercial Banks, which also covers banks that offer digital banking services). Locally incorporated banks (Badan Hukum Indonesia/BHI) may be established and/or owned by:

Question: description: Patent enforcement issues: civil and administrative procedures and remedies, provisional and other measures
Impact:
In Indonesia's current legislation covers civil and administrative remedies and provisional measures in the context of patent enforcement and protection. 

Article 47 (UU Nomor 13 Tahun 2016) allows for substantive examination procedures. Article 132 (UU Nomor 13 Tahun 2016) provides the basis for filing civil suits for patent infringement. However, these civil provisions do not specify expedited civil relief or injunctions within standard procedures, indicating a lack of structured civil remedies aimed explicitly at rapid enforcement. Thus,  provides only the right for patent holders to initiate civil lawsuits for damages due to patent infringement, covering civil remedies.

UU Nomor 65 Tahun 2024 (the latest amendment to the patent law) details administrative processes. There are limited administrative pathways, such as appeals to the Patent Appeal Commission (Komisi Banding Paten) for specific decisions, but this is not equivalent to the broader administrative enforcement seen in some other jurisdictions. Article 120, UU Nomor 65 Tahun 2024 includes the option for administrative action by the Directorate General of Intellectual Property (DGIP), which oversees patent administration but does not specify immediate administrative remedies for enforcement. 

Essentially, in Indonesia, legal remedies concerning intellectual property - particularly through litigation - are submitted to the Commercial Court. as of now, there are no specific procedural rules governing proceedings in the Commercial Court, so cases continue to follow the general civil procedure law. 

Additionally, provisional measures are explicitly provided for under Law Number 13 of 2016 on Patents, which remains in effect. The Law provides a mechanism for provisional or emergency measures in responsee to potential or ongoing patent infringements. Specifically, Chapter XIV on PROVISIONAL DETERMINATION BY THE COURT, in Article 155, which states: 
At the request of the party suffering losses due to the implementation of the Patent, the Commercial Court may issue a provisional determination to:
a.	prevent the entry of goods suspected of infringing the Patent and/or related rights.
b.	secure and prevent the removal of evidence by alleged infringer; and/or
c.	halt the infringement in order to prevent further losses.

Question: description: Not in the WIPO Copyright Treaty (WCT)
Source Legislation:
Patent Cooperation Treaty;

Presidential Decree No. 16 of 1997 on the Ratification of the Patent Cooperation Treaty
Impact:
Indonesia is one of the Contracting States to the Patent Cooperation Treaty. However, Indonesia does not consider itself bound by Article 59 (related to any dispute between any Contracting State having made such a declaration and any other Contracting State).

Presidential Decree No. 16 of 1997 on the Ratification of the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) and its regulations expressly sets forth Indonesia’s position with regard to Article 59 of the PCT. The Decree states that Indonesia does not consider itself bound by Article 59, which relates to the settlement of disputes between Contracting States, particularly those concerning the interpretation or application of the PCT and its regulations.

Article 59 of the PCT provides that disputes between Contracting States should be resolved through negotiation, or if that fails, by submission to the International Court of Justice (ICJ). By reserving its position and opting not to be bound by this provision, Indonesia has effectively excluded itself from the default dispute resolution mechanism under the PCT.

As a result, any disputes involving Indonesia and other PCT Contracting States regarding the interpretation or application of the Treaty cannot be brought before the ICJ based on Article 59 alone, unless Indonesia expressly agrees to such a procedure in a separate arrangement.

The decision emphasized the need for updated regulations to ensure digital platforms prevent and address copyright violations effectively

Question: description: Mandatory disclosure of trade secrets, such as source code and algorithms
Impact:
There are no provisions governing the disclosure of trade secrets (including source code) in the context of trade conducted through electronic systems under Government Regulation Number 80 of 2019 or Minister of Trade Regulation Number 31 of 2023. Government Regulation No.82 of 2012 as replaced by the Government Regulation No.71/2019 requires that providers of bespoke software provide or escrow the source codes associated with their service.

In Indonesia, the mandatory disclosure of trade secrets, including source code and algorithms, is primarily governed by the Law No. 30 of 2000 on Trade Secrets and Government Regulation No. 82 of 2012 on the Implementation of Electronic Systems and Transactions. While there is no broad requirement for mandatory disclosure of trade secrets in Indonesia. 

Law No. 30 of 2000 on Trade Secrets:
Article 1: Defines trade secrets and establishes the criteria for what constitutes a trade secret, emphasizing that it must be kept confidential and not generally known to the public.
Article 3: States that trade secrets are protected as long as they are kept confidential and have economic value. This implies that there is no general requirement for mandatory disclosure unless specified by law.
Article 11: Allows the holder of a trade secret to file a lawsuit against anyone who unlawfully discloses or uses the trade secret. This reinforces the idea that trade secrets should not be disclosed without consent.
Article 14 implies that a violation occurs if someone obtains or controls a trade secret in a manner contrary to the law.
Article 17 states that any person who deliberately and without rights uses the trade secret of another party, or conducts any acts as referred to in Article 13 or Article 14, can be sentenced to imprisonment of up to 2 years and/or a fine of up to 300 million rupiah.

Government Regulation No. 82 of 2012:
Article 8: Requires providers of electronic systems to submit source code and documentation to the relevant government agency when developing software for public institutions. 
Article 9: Mandates that providers must ensure the confidentiality of the source code used in their systems, indicating that while there may be a requirement to disclose to certain authorities, the confidentiality of that information must still be maintained.
Article 29: States that for criminal proceedings, electronic system providers must provide information contained in their systems upon lawful request from investigators.
The regulation does not impose any mandatory disclosure of trade secrets. Instead, it provides strong protections to ensure that the confidentiality of trade secrets is maintained during administrative, investigative, and legal processes.

Government Regulation No. 71 of 2019
Article 9: Developers of software specifically created for Penyelenggara Sistem Elektronik Lingkup Publik (Public Sector Electronic System Providers) are required to submit the source code and documentation of the software to the relevant public institution or agency.
If the public institution or agency does not have the infrastructure to store the source code, the developer must submit it to a trusted third party (source code escrow).
The developer must ensure that the source code and documentation are accessible to the trusted third party and guarantee its confidentiality. The source code is to be used only for the purposes of the public sector entity.

Question: description: Lack of effective trade secrets legal framework
Source Legislation: Law No.30 on Trade Secret 2000
Impact:
Indonesia has a specific law (Law No. 30 of 2000) that defines trade secrets, outlines the rights of trade secret holders, and provides mechanisms for protection and enforcement. This indicates that there is a legal framework in place. The law provides clear definitions of what constitutes a trade secret and the conditions under which it is protected. Trade Secrets are legally defined as information in the field of technology and/or business that is not known by the public and has economic values as it is useful in business activities, and the confidentiality of which is maintained by its owner (Article 1). Trade secrets are protected as long as they are kept confidential and have economic value. This implies that there is no general requirement for mandatory disclosure unless specified by law (Article 3). It includes provisions Rights of Trade Secret Holders: Owners have the right to use, license, or prevent unauthorized use of their trade secrets (Articles 4 and 6). And the law allows trade secret holders to seek legal remedies against unauthorized disclosure or use (Articles 11 and 12). 

The law includes specific provisions regarding the rights of trade secret holders, the conditions for protection, and the legal recourse available in cases of infringement. Any person who deliberately and without rights uses the Trade Secret of another party, or conducts any acts as referred to in Article 13 or Article 14 of Law No. 30 shall be sentenced to imprisonment of at most 2 (two) years and/or a fine (Article 17). 

However, the law lacks implementing regulations, and there is no discovery procedure provided. As a result, certain aspects—such as the mechanism or parameters for proving violations—are not yet clearly regulated. The effectiveness of these provisions can vary in practice, indicating that while there is a framework, it may not be fully effective in all situations. The Law does not explicitly mention the lack of a discovery procedure, but it is a known issue in many legal systems that do not have robust discovery processes. This can make it difficult to prove that a trade secret was unlawfully obtained, especially if the suspected party had a prior relationship or access to the trade secret.

Impact:

Article 149 states that the definitions and regulatory framework for postal, telecommunications, broadcasting, and electronic transactions follow the relevant sectoral laws, including the Telecommunications Law No. 36 of 1999, the Broadcasting Law No. 32 of 2002, and the Electronic Information and Transactions Law No. 11 of 2008. Article 151 focuses on compliance, monitoring, and sanctions for telecommunications businesses. Operators must adhere to technical, security, and service quality standards set by the Ministry of Communications and Informatics, with periodic audits and performance reviews. Impact:
Indonesia's approach to cross-border data policies is primarily governed by the Personal Data Protection Law (PDP Law), which was enacted in 2022 and is set to be fully enforced by October 2024. The Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) of 2022 is Indonesia’s first comprehensive law dedicated specifically to personal data protection. It significantly updates and consolidates personal data governance compared to Law No. 11 of 2008 on Electronic Information and Transactions (EIT Law) and Government Regulation No. 82 of 2012 (Regulation 82). The PDPA does not fully replace the EIT Law or Regulation 82, but it supersedes and updates many of their provisions related to data privacy, creating a more robust framework for data protection. 

Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA), 2022 does not mandate strict localization but emphasizes secure data transfer practices.
Under Article 55, the PDPA allows cross-border data transfers but imposes conditions to ensure that the data is protected according to Indonesian standards. Transfers are allowed if the destination country has an equivalent level of data protection, or contractual safeguards are in place to protect the data.

Article 56 states that the Data Controller may transfer personal data to other Data Controllers and/or Data Processors outside the jurisdiction of the Republic of Indonesia in accordance with the provisions regulated in this law. It emphasizes that when transferring personal data, the Data Controller must ensure that the country where the receiving Data Controller and/or Data Processor is located provides an adequate level of personal data protection. If the level of protection is not adequate, the Data Controller must ensure that there are adequate and binding safeguards in place. If neither condition is met, explicit consent from the data subject must be obtained for the transfer.

Article 66 addresses requirements for data security and confidentiality, essential for sectors handling sensitive data, like banking and finance, mandating that personal data be processed securely to protect against unauthorized access. Articles 65 and 67 prohibit unauthorized collection, disclosure, or usage of personal data, establishing penalties for non-compliance, which directly affects financial service providers’ handling of customer data.

Article 74 of transitional Provisions states that existing data controllers and processors must comply with the new law within two years of its enactment (October 2024), allowing time for organizations to adjust their practices.

Impact:
The Minister of Communication and Informatics Regulation No.20 of 2016 provides a legal framework for the protection of the use of personal data through electronic systems. The Government Regulation No. 40 of 2019 further clarifies the definition of personal data to be protected that include fingerprint, signature, iris (in eyes), disgraces, notes on mental or physical diseases.

Moreover, Law No. 27 establishes a general framework for the protection of personal data in Indonesia. It is closely aligned with international data privacy standards, and is largely modelled on the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation. Data controllers, data processors and relevant parties that process personal data are given a two year transition period following the enactment of Law No. 27, thus up to 17 October 2024 to conform with it. Once the transition period elapses, all such parties must comply with all the provisions of Law No. 27 and any noncompliance thereto may possibly be enforced.

Indonesia enacted the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) of 2022, establishing Indonesia’s first dedicated and comprehensive data protection framework, akin to international standards like the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Key features of the PDPA include:
	1.	Clear Definition of Personal Data and Comprehensive Rights for Data Subjects:
Article 6: Grants data subjects the right to correct and update their data.
Article 8: Provides the right to request the deletion or termination of processing personal data.
Article 9: Allows withdrawal of consent for data processing.
Article 11: Allows data subjects to limit or suspend the processing of their data
	2.	Cross-Border Transfer Rules: Allows data transfers abroad under strict conditions, ensuring equivalent protection.
Article 55: Governs cross-border transfers, permitting them only if the destination country has adequate protection measures or appropriate safeguards are in place
	3.	Data Processing Obligations: Imposes duties on data controllers and processors for secure and lawful data handling.
Article 35: Requires data controllers to implement organizational and technical measures to ensure data protection.
Article 39: Mandates appointment of a Data Protection Officer (DPO) for entities processing sensitive data or conducting large-scale processing.
Articles 40–42: Specify reporting obligations in case of data breaches, ensuring accountability and transparency
	4.	Enforcement and Penalties: Provides for administrative sanctions and criminal penalties for violations.
Article 67: Imposes administrative fines for non-compliance.
Articles 66–68: Stipulate criminal penalties for unauthorized access, misuse, or other breaches of personal data 

However, the PDPA is still being operationalized and will fully come into effect in October 2024, alongside sector-specific regulations (e.g., financial and health) that augment its application. While this indicates progress, Indonesia’s data protection regime is still evolving and may face challenges in enforcement and harmonization across sectors.

Question: description: Lack of safe harbour for copyright infringements
Impact:
Domestic and/or foreign Electronic System Operators in Trade (PPMSE), as well as Intermediary Service Providers, are held liable for any legal consequences arising from the presence of illegal electronic information content.
However, this liability does not apply if the respective domestic and/or foreign PPMSE acts promptly to remove electronic links and/or illegal electronic information content upon acquiring actual knowledge or awareness of such content.

This provision does not apply to Intermediary Service Providers acting in the following capacities:
a.	As a mere conduit, meaning they only transmit information and: (1) Do not initiate the transmission; (2) Do not select the receiver of the transmission; and (3) Do not modify the information being transmitted.
b.	As a caching provider, meaning they temporarily store information solely for the efficiency of communications, provided that they: (1) Do not modify the stored information; (2) Comply with conditions on accessing such information; (3) Follow rules for updating information in accordance with widely accepted industry standards; (4) Do not interfere with lawful technologies widely used in the industry to obtain data on the use of such information; and (5) Act promptly to delete or disable access to stored information upon gaining actual knowledge that the original source has removed or disabled access to such information, or upon order by a court or authority.
c.	As a hosting provider, meaning they offer storage space for the placement or uploading of content, and: (1) Have no actual knowledge of illegal acts or information, and if there is a claim for damages, the provider was not aware of the illegal nature of the act or content; or (2) Upon acquiring such knowledge or awareness, the provider acts promptly to remove or disable access to the content.
d.	As a search engine, which functions as a provider, finder, or crawler of information and networks.
Additionally, intermediary service providers offering interactive computer services shall not be held liable or subject to legal claims for actions taken to restrict or remove access to content, if:
●	The action was voluntarily taken in good faith to restrict access to or availability of material that the user or provider believes falls under the category of illegal electronic content, without requiring a legal determination of its protected status; or
●	The action was taken to restrict public access, disable, or make such content inaccessible, either based on the provider’s own assessment or that of a third party.

Question: description: Lack of safe harbour for copyright infringements
Source Legislation: Copyright Law No.28 2014
Impact:
In Indonesia, the concept of safe harbor for copyright infringements is primarily addressed under the Law Number 28 of 2014 on Copyrights. However, the law itself does not explicitly use the term "safe harbor" as it is commonly understood in jurisdictions like the United States under the DMCA. Instead, the Indonesian law provides a framework that indirectly supports the concept through its provisions on intermediary liability and the responsibilities of online platforms. The relevant provisions in the Indonesian Copyright Law that relate to the responsibilities of online platforms and could be interpreted as providing a form of safe harbor include:
- Article 10 outlines the rights and obligations of copyright holders and users, which can indirectly affect how platforms manage user-generated content and copyright infringements.
- Article 43 discusses the limitations and exceptions to copyright, which may include provisions that affect how online platforms handle content.
- Article 44 provides for the protection of technological measures and rights management information, which can be relevant to how platforms manage and protect copyrighted content.
- Article 55 outlines the liability of service providers. It states that service providers are not liable for copyright infringement if they can demonstrate that they did not have knowledge of the infringing activity and acted promptly to remove or disable access to the infringing content upon receiving a notice.

Question: description: Lack of safe harbour for copyright infringements
Impact:
Law No. 11 of 2008 on Information and Electronic Transactions (ITE Law). The ITE Law is another important piece of legislation that governs electronic transactions and online content in Indonesia. It does not explicitly offer a safe harbor for online platforms in the context of copyright infringement, but it touches on issues related to online content and its regulation.
- Article 15 discusses the liability of electronic system providers. It states that they are responsible for the operation of their systems but are not liable for user-generated content if they can prove that the infringement was due to force majeure, user error, or negligence on the part of the user.
- Article 27 (1) Prohibits the distribution of content that infringes on another’s rights, including intellectual property rights. This could apply to online platforms, but it does not specify the liability of platforms for user-uploaded infringing content.
- Article 28 elaborates on the prohibition of content that violates the law, including defamation, obscenity, or the infringement of intellectual property rights. Again, this article does not address safe harbor provisions or limitations on platform liability.
- Article 29 Imposes obligations on service providers to ensure their services do not violate laws, which might include copyright infringement, but it does not include protections or exemptions for service providers.

Question: description: Export restrictions on ICTgoods and online services
Impact:
The Circular of the Minister of Communication and Information Technology No. 5/ 2016 provides the exemption to e-commerce providers from the liability for failures to comply with the relevant laws in the event of force majeure, errors, or negligence. E-commerce providers will only be responsible for prohibited content posted on their platform if they are unable to prove that the uploading of such content was caused by the users.

Government Regulation No.80/2019 provides a broad immunity to e-commerce service providers and intermediary service providers from the legal consequences arising from illegal third-party content. For e-commerce service providers, the regulation discharges them from any liability for illegal content found on their platforms, provided they have acted expeditiously to remove or disable access to such content after knowing of its existence (either by way of a report from a third party or finding it out themselves). To ensure that an e-commerce service provider is alerted of illegal content on its platform, the regulation requires such provider to provide terms of use/terms and conditions of the platform to its users and employing certain technology and/or feature in the platform for users to submit a report. For intermediary service providers, the regulation discharges them from any liability for illegal content provided that such providers are acting as a mere conduit. This will be evidenced by, among others, the provider's lack of control over the transmission. If an intermediary service provider provides an 'interactive computer service', such as a social media platform, they will be discharged from any liability for restricting or removing access to content if such action was carried out in good faith and based on a report that such content is illegal.

MOCI Regulation 5 now provides that private ESOs hosting user-generated content may be exempted from legal liability for prohibited content transmitted or distributed on their electronic systems as long as they have fulfilled their governance obligations, shared information on subscribers who uploaded the prohibited content for monitoring and law enforcement purposes, and taken down the prohibited content as regulated under MOCI Regulation 5. Private ESOs must ensure that their electronic systems do not (i) contain prohibited electronic information or documents and (ii) facilitate dissemination of prohibited electronic information or documents. They also must take down prohibited content within 24 hours or four hours (the latter is for urgent prohibited content, such as child pornography content, terrorism content and content that causes public unrest, which is very broad) after receiving the takedown notice. MOCI Regulation 5 classifies prohibited content into content that:
- is in violation of laws and regulations
- causes anxiety for society and disturbs public order based on the government’s assessment
- posts or provides access to prohibited content.

Question: description: Local content requirements
Impact:

Question: description: Lack of transparent technical standards
Impact:
Law No.20 of 2014 states that Indonesia National Standards (SNI) can be developed in accordance with the international standards by taking into account the considerations of national interest and global competition. 

The development of Indonesian National Standard (SNI) is regulated under the Regulation of the National Standardization Body Number 8 of 2022. This regulation does not stipulate that stakeholders involved in the development of SNI originate solely from within the country. However, they are required to meet the stipulated criteria.

The formulation of the Indonesian National Standard (SNI) is carried out in a transparent manner and is accessible to the public via https://sispk.bsn.go.id. The public may provide input and feedback on the Draft SNI under development during the public enquiry stage.

Law No. 20/2014 on Standardization and Conformity Assessment establishes the framework for standardization and conformity assessment. It requires that regulated products meet mandatory SNI and undergo conformity assessment. Article 5 stipulates that technical standards should prioritize “national interests,” which can implicitly limit foreign participation in the process. And Article 8 outlines the formation of technical committees (komite teknis), which are predominantly comprised of local experts, without explicit provisions for foreign stakeholders. Article 41 states that technical standards should be based on consultation, but there is no explicit mechanism for notifying foreign stakeholders or publishing drafts for review.

Government Regulation No. 34/2018 on Trade Goods Certification and Standardization which serves as an implementing regulation for the provisions outlined in Law No. 20/2014, provides detailed rules and operational guidelines for enforcing the law, particularly concerning trade goods that must meet mandatory SNI or other technical standards.

Question: description: Deviation from international encryption standards (ISO, IEC, ITU, FIPS, AES, TDES, and ECC)
Impact:
Indonesia has the SNI ISO/IEC 19790:2015 standard, which regulates information technology, security techniques, and security requirements for cryptographic modules (ISO/IEC 19790:2012, IDT). 

The National Cyber and Crypto Agency (BSSN) is currently preparing a draft Agency Regulation concerning the Implementation of Indonesian Cryptographic Algorithms and the Cryptographic Module Security Assessment Scheme. The regulatory substance includes: general criteria and specific criteria for Indonesian cryptographic algorithms, the Indonesian cryptographic committee, and the cryptographic module security certification scheme. In this regulation, SNI ISO/IEC 19790:2015 is required to be implemented by Electronic System Operators (PSE) on Vital Information Infrastructure (IIV) protection technology.

Based on Presidential Regulation No. 47/2023 on the National Cybersecurity Strategy and Cyber Crisis Management, Indonesia emphasizes the importance of maintaining cybersecurity, including through regulations governing the use of encryption. This regulation is explicitly outlined in Article 6 of Presidential Regulation 47/2023, which addresses national cryptographic independence. Currently, Indonesia has formally adopted a national encryption policy framework that “deviates” in the sense that it emphasizes the use of domestically developed cryptographic algorithms, as stipulated in the Regulation of the National Cyber and Crypto Agency (BSSN) No. 11 of 2024 on the Implementation of Indonesian Cryptographic Algorithms and Cryptographic Module Security Conformity Assessment. This policy can be implemented by Electronic System Operators (PSE) or Critical Information Infrastructure Operators (PIIV). 

As outlined in BSSN Regulation No. 11/2024, the reference standard used is SNI ISO/IEC 19790:2015 Information Technology — Security Techniques — Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules, and the adoption of international cryptographic systems remains possible. According to BSSN Regulation No. 11/2024, there is no application of encryption standards that deviate from internationally recognized standards. Furthermore, under the Electronic Information and Transactions Law (ITE Law) and BSSN Regulation No. 11/2024, foreign encryption products are required to undergo a certification process before being used in Indonesia. 

Although there is no explicit obligation to disclose trade secrets, the certification process may require the submission of proprietary technical documentation, which can raise concerns about the protection of sensitive business information. Essentially, these regulations aim to ensure that products and services comply with adopted security standards. It can be concluded that these policies are not intended to serve as a direct barrier to digital trade, as the regulations remain aligned with international standards and do not mandate the disclosure of trade secrets during the certification process.

There is no explicit mandate in Indonesian law or regulations requiring the use of a .id domain name for foreign or domestic e-commerce businesses. However, the Government Regulation No.80/2019 encourages its use as part of creating a local digital presence.

Under the Regulation No.80/2019, e-commerce law states that subject to certain thresholds, foreign business actors that actively conduct e-commerce activities with consumers in Indonesia are deemed as physically present in Indonesia and conducting fixed business activities in Indonesia. These thresholds are related to (i) number of transactions, (ii) transaction value, (iii) number of shipped packages, and/or (iv) volume of traffic or number of users. A foreign business actor that meets any of the thresholds must appoint an Indonesian representative that can act on its behalf.

The regulation includes provisions related to the use of local domain names. Specifically, Article 21 of Government Regulation No. 80 of 2019 mandates the prioritization of using Indonesia’s top-level domain name (".id") for Electronic Systems in the form of websites. It also establishes sanctions for violations of this obligation, which may include: written warnings; inclusion in the priority monitoring list; inclusion in the blacklist; temporary blocking of domestic and/or foreign PPMSE services by the relevant authorized agency; and/or revocation of business licenses. 

Article 7 specifies that foreign electronic system operators that meet certain criteria (such as transaction volume or user base) are considered to have a physical presence in Indonesia. These operators are required to appoint a local representative who can act on their behalf within the country.The specific criteria for foreign PPMSEs, as referred to in Article 18 of Minister of Trade Regulation No. 31 of 2023, include: (a) having conducted transactions with at least 1,000 consumers within a one-year period; (b) having delivered at least 1,000 packages to consumers within a one-year period; and/or (c) having at least 1% of domestic internet users accessing their platform within a one-year period.

Question: description: Local presence requirements for online service providers
Impact:
The Minister of Communication and Informatics Regulation No. 5 of 2020, as amended by the The Minister of Communication and Informatics Regulation No. 10 of 2021 on Private Electronic System Operators mandates foreign Private Electronic System Operators (ESOs) to register their businesses to the relevant ministry through the online single submission system. ESOs should also appoint liaison officers, who have to be domiciled in Indonesia. The duty of the liaison officer is to facilitate any access request by government authorities and takedown request. According to the regulation, ESOs are persons, business entities, or communities that operate an electronic system. ESOs include electronic system operators that are supervised by ministers or institutions in accordance with laws and regulations, and electronic system operators that have an online portal, site, or application through the internet. The requirement was first enacted with the Government Regulation No. 71/2019 regarding the Provision of Electronic System and Transaction.

For foreign electronic system operators, Article 4 (MOCI 5/2020) outlines that they must register if they provide services in Indonesia, conduct business in Indonesia, or have systems used or offered in Indonesia. This implies a need for some form of local presence, but it does not specify the requirement for a physical office or other commercial presence beyond registration.

Question: description: Local presence requirements for online service providers
Source Legislation:
Regulation of the Minister of Communication and Informatics of the Republic of Indonesia No.5 on Private Electronic System Operators 2020;

Minister of Communication and Informatics Regulation No. 10 on the Amendment to Minister of Communication and Informatics Regulation No. 5 of 2020 on Private Electronic System Operators 2021
Impact:
Digital service providers such as social media platforms, electronic commerce providers, and over-the-top (OTT) media services are required to register with the Ministry of Communication and Information under Article 2 of MOCI 5/2020. Additionally, these entities must establish a representative office in Indonesia.

For foreign electronic system operators, Article 4 (MOCI 5/2020) outlines that they must register if they provide services in Indonesia, conduct business in Indonesia, or have systems used or offered in Indonesia. This implies a need for some form of local presence, but it does not specify the requirement for a physical office or other commercial presence beyond registration.

While MOCI Regulation No. 5/2020 required foreign PSEs to register and implied the need for a local presence, Regulation No. 10/2021 did not explicitly mandate the establishment of a physical representative office in Indonesia. Instead, the focus is now on mandatory registration with the Ministry of Communication and Informatics (Kominfo) through the OSS RBA system and compliance with Indonesian laws, such as content moderation and taxation. There is no explicit requirement for a physical office or representative office in Indonesia under the updated regulations.

Note that Minister of Communication and Informatics Regulation No. 5/2020, last amended by the Indonesia Minister of Communication and Informatics Regulation No. 10/2021.

Question: description: Lack of legal framework for online consumer protection
Source Legislation: Law No.8 on Consumer Protection 1999
Impact:
Indonesia's Consumer Protection Law No. 8 is a comprehensive framework aimed at protecting consumer rights, ensuring transparency, and mandating the safety and quality of goods and services in electronic commerce. However, it does not raise specific e-commerce or distance sales issues. The Law forms the foundation of consumer protection in Indonesia.
- Article 4 enumerates consumer rights, including the right to safety, accurate information, and compensation for damages.
- Article 7 imposes obligations on businesses to provide clear, truthful information about goods/services and to guarantee their safety.
- Article 8 prohibits businesses from offering goods/services that fail to meet safety, quality, or labeling standards.

It is important to note that the Consumer Protection Law is the legal basis for the implementation of consumer protection in Indonesia, although it does not specifically regulate online consumer protection.

Question: description: Lack of legal framework for online consumer protection
Impact:
Law (Law) No. 19 of 2016, Amendments to Law Number 11 of 2008 concerning Information and Electronic Transactions addresses digital and electronic transactions:
- Article 9 ensures consumer protection in electronic contracts, mandating transparency and clarity in terms and conditions.
- Article 18 governs the validity of electronic contracts, emphasizing fairness and requiring accessibility to contract information by consumers.

Moreover, the mechanism for regulating electronic contracts can also be found in Chapter X of Government Regulation No. 80 of 2019.

Question: description: Lack of legal framework for online consumer protection
Source Legislation: Regulation of the Government of the Republic of Indonesia No.80 on Trading Through the Electronic System (E-commerce Law) 2019
Impact:
Government Regulation No. 80 of 2019 explicitly stipulates that foreign Electronic System Operators in Trade (PPMSE) that meet certain criteria are deemed to have a physical presence in Indonesia and are therefore required to appoint a representative domiciled in Indonesia:
●	The obligation to provide consumer complaint services is stipulated in Article 27. 
●	The obligation to display clear and accurate product information is regulated in Article 13.
●	Article 53 states that an electronic contract must include information on the procedure for returning goods and/or services in case of any discrepancies between what was received and what was agreed upon. However, the mechanism that is explicitly detailed pertains to the refund process, as outlined in Article 71.
●	Article 32 relates to Electronic Advertising, the provisions concerning consumer rights in Electronic System-Based Trading (PPMSE) are found in Article 26. This article requires Business Actors to protect consumer rights in accordance with the prevailing laws and regulations on consumer protection;
●	One of the key consumer rights under the Consumer Protection Law (UUPK) is the right to receive compensation, reimbursement, and/or replacement if the goods and/or services received do not match the agreement or are not delivered as promised.

In addition, PPMSE conducting business activities in the context of electronic commerce (PMSE) are obligated to comply with business licensing requirements in accordance with the prevailing laws and regulations.

Furthermore, Minister of Trade Regulation No. 31 of 2023 serves as a regulatory framework for the governance of PMSE, aiming to establish a healthy digital trade ecosystem and ensure consumer protection, while taking into account the ever-evolving nature of PMSE business models.

It is important to note that Regulation 31/2023 does not stand alone, but rather refers to and aligns with other relevant laws and regulations, including those governing goods distribution, electronic system operators, and others.
